blocks.prompt: The Wooden Box That Sings
blocks.text: A violin is a wooden box with a long neck. It has four strings. A player pulls a bow across the strings. The bow is not made of string. It is strung with hair from the tail of a real horse. On its own, that hair would just slide. So the player rubs it with rosin, a hard lump of tree sap, to help it grab. Now the hair grabs the string and lets go, again and again, very fast. That makes the string shake. The shaking travels down into the wooden box, and the box shakes the air inside it. The air pushes out through two holes shaped like the letter f. That is the sound you hear.

3.title: The Wooden Box That Sings

blocks.prompt: The Box Does the Singing
blocks.text: Pluck a violin string on its own and you hear almost nothing. A string is thin. It cannot push much air, and pushing air is what making sound really means. So the violin cheats. Under the strings sits a thin piece of maple called the bridge. The strings press down on it. When a string shakes, the bridge shakes, and the bridge is glued to nothing. It just stands there, held up by the pull of the strings. The bridge passes the shaking into the front of the violin, which is a thin sheet of spruce wood. Now a wide piece of wood is moving the air instead of a thin string. Inside the box, a little wooden rod called the soundpost carries the shaking through to the back. The whole box breathes. Air rushes in and out of the two f shaped holes. That is why a violin is loud enough to fill a hall, and why a violin with a crack in it sounds wrong.

blocks.prompt: Why the Bow Has to Be Sticky
blocks.text: A bow looks simple. A stick of wood, about one hundred and fifty hairs from a horse's tail pulled tight along it, and that is all. Look closer and the bow turns out to be doing something clever, hundreds of times a second. Draw a bow slowly across a string and you might expect the hair to slide, the way a hand slides down a banister. It does not. Before playing, the violinist rubs the hair with rosin, a hard amber lump of pine sap boiled down until it sets. Rosin makes the hair grip. So the hair catches the string and drags it sideways. The string stretches, resists, and finally snaps back past the hair. Then the hair catches it again. Grab, release, grab, release. On the A string of a violin, that cycle repeats four hundred and forty times every second, and each snap is a tiny pulse of energy fed into the instrument. Scientists call it stick slip motion. A creaking door hinge and a squeaking chalkboard do the same thing. The violin just does it on purpose, and in tune. That is also why a brand new bow, straight from the shop, makes no sound worth hearing. The hair is clean. It slides. Without rosin, a bow is only a stick with hair on it.

blocks.prompt: The Little Town That Made the Best Violins
blocks.text: In the middle of the 1500s, in a small town in northern Italy called Cremona, a maker named Andrea Amati settled on a shape. Four strings, a waisted body, a curved top carved from spruce, a back and sides of maple, and two holes cut in the shape of the letter f. His oldest surviving violins were built in the 1560s. Nearly five hundred years later, the violin in a school orchestra today is still recognizably his design. Almost nothing else people used in the 1560s has survived unchanged. Cremona kept its advantage for two hundred years. The Amati workshop trained others. The most famous was Antonio Stradivari, who worked in the town until he died in 1737, in his nineties. He built well over a thousand instruments, and about six hundred and fifty of them still exist. Another Cremona maker, Giuseppe Guarneri, built fewer and died younger, and his violins are rarer still. Then the town's run ended. Nobody has ever explained why the great ones cluster in one place, in one span of years, in a handful of workshops. The instruments became legends, and legends get expensive. In 2011 a Stradivari violin known as the Lady Blunt sold for about sixteen million dollars. Soloists who cannot afford one borrow from banks and foundations, playing for decades on an instrument they will never own. For a long time the explanation for the price was the sound. Everyone knew a Stradivari sounded better. Wood grown slowly in a colder climate, a secret varnish, a lost recipe: the theories multiplied, and none was ever proven. Then researchers ran the obvious test. In 2012, and again in 2014, the scientist Claudia Fritz asked skilled violinists to play old Italian instruments and modern ones in a darkened room, wearing goggles, unable to see what was in their hands. The players could not reliably tell which was which. On average, they slightly preferred the new violins. That result did not lower any prices. It suggests that part of what people hear in a Stradivari is the label, the story, and the four hundred year old wood glowing under stage lights. It also suggests something more cheerful. If the best violins are not a lost secret, then the makers working today, in Cremona and everywhere else, are not chasing a ghost. They may already have caught it.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Around 70 separate pieces of wood, joined with hide glue
Spruce top, maple back and sides, ebony fingerboard
Bridge and soundpost are held by pressure alone

blocks.prompt: Seventy Pieces of Wood and One Argument
blocks.text: A violin is about seventy separate pieces of wood, joined with hide glue that can be melted apart again by anyone who needs to open the instrument up. It weighs less than a can of soup. It has no electronics, no valves, no reeds, and no frets to tell your fingers where the notes are. It has barely changed since the 1560s. And a good one can be heard clearly at the back of a hall over an orchestra of a hundred players. Understanding how is a lesson in how sound actually works. Start with the string. A bowed string is a terrible loudspeaker. It is thin, so it slices through air rather than pushing it, and pushing air is the entire business of sound. Left to itself, a vibrating string is nearly silent. What the violin does, essentially, is convert a small fast motion into a large slow one, then hand it to something wide enough to shove air around. The chain runs like this. Rosin on the bow hair grips the string, drags it sideways, and lets it snap back, hundreds of times a second. The string's vibration passes into the bridge, a carved slip of maple two inches high that is not glued to anything and stands upright purely under the downward pressure of the strings. The bridge rocks. Its feet press into the top plate, a thin sheet of spruce chosen because spruce carries sound along its grain faster than almost any other wood while staying feather light. Inside the box, wedged between the top and the back and again held by nothing but friction, stands a rod of spruce called the soundpost. The French call it the soul. It couples the two plates so the whole body flexes, and it stiffens the top exactly under the treble foot of the bridge, so the top pivots rather than simply bouncing. The box now breathes. Air pumps in and out of the two f holes, and the enclosed air resonates like the note you get blowing across a bottle. Every one of those parts is a compromise. A thicker top is stronger and duller. A thinner top is louder and closer to breaking. Move the soundpost two millimeters and the instrument changes character. The maker is not carving a shape so much as tuning a system, mostly by tapping the wood and listening to it. The f holes are the strangest evidence that this tuning was found by trial rather than theory. In 2015, engineers at MIT measured hundreds of instruments built between the Amati workshop of the 1560s and Stradivari's shop around 1700, and found that the holes had grown steadily longer and narrower. That change matters, because air moves fastest at the edges of an opening, so the sound power a violin radiates depends on the perimeter of the hole rather than its area. Nobody in Cremona knew fluid dynamics. Makers copied instruments they liked, copied them imperfectly, kept the accidents that sounded better, and over roughly a century random error walked the design uphill toward a solution the mathematics only confirmed four hundred years later. That is the argument worth having about violins. The famous story says a genius in Cremona had a secret. The evidence says something less romantic and more interesting: a craft tradition, copying itself with small errors and keeping whatever worked, arrived at an answer no single person inside it could have reasoned out.
